## Live-Attenuated Vaccines

## Never give live vaccines to:

- $ Pregnant patients
- $ People who are immunocompromised
- Live-attenuated vaccines:
- $ Weakened versions of live virus
- $ Must replicate in the body to produce immunity
- Viral replication reaction (fever, rash)

- Vaccines are valid if given 4 days prior to the scheduled time.
- Vaccines given 5 days prior to the scheduled time are invalid.

## CDC Advice: How to Address Caregiver Concerns About Vaccines

- Take time to listen to concerns.
- Solicit and welcome questions.
- Keep the conversation going.
- Respect caregivers' authority.
- Reduce the stress of shots.
- Visit CDC for specific recommendations.
- Acknowledge benefits and risks.

## What If They Still Refuse to Vaccinate?

- Excluding children from your practice: not recommended!
- Teach about the clinical presentations of vaccine-preventable diseases.
- Remind caregivers to call before bringing child to office visit if child is ill.
- Alert other health care providers about which patients are not immunized.
- Sign CDC's refusal-to-vaccinate form.

- Infection of the middle ear
- Etiology

Neurodevelopmental disorder

## NOTES Headaches

- Common
- >90% of school-age children
- Most common:
- $ Migraine, tension, cluster, chronic daily headache
- Secondary headaches:
- $ uncommon
- Benign headaches: Viral illness, stress, eye strain

## Headaches: History and Physical

## Imaging

- MRI preferred unless something is rapidly developing
- Red flags
- Abnormal PE/neuro exam
- Underlying disease (e.g., sickle cell, immune deficiency)

## History

- Headache:
- $ Pattern
- $ History
- $ Burden
- Family
- Past medical
- Current medications

## Physical exam

- Head circumference
- Height/weight trajectories
- Thorough EENT exam
- Comprehensive neurologic exam

<!-- image -->

## Headache Red Flags

Worrisome for pathologic intracranial process

- Headache awakens child (other signs of increased intracranial pressure)
- Thunderclap headache
- Associated neuro findings
- $ Persistent nausea, vomiting
- $ Altered mental status
- $ Ataxia
- Recurrent localized headache, chronic progressive headache pattern
- Age <6 years (inadequate history)
- Personality changes
- Absent family history of migraine

<!-- image -->

## Migraine Headaches

- Most common acute recurrent headache in children
- Follow ICHD-3 criteria for diagnosis.
- Accompanied by nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain
- Auras are common in children.

## Migraine Management

- Nonpharmacologic
- $ Eliminate triggers
- $ Stress reduction
- $ Rest
- Pharmacologic: Prophylactic
- $ Cyproheptadine syrup (for young children)
- $ Vitamin B 2 , melatonin, magnesium (safe/well tolerated)

<!-- image -->

## Acute Symptomatic Seizure

- Provoked by an acute physiologic state
- $ Electrolyte abnormalities: hyponatremia, hypocalcemia
- $ Fever: "febrile seizures"
- $ Toxin exposure
- $ Acute intracranial inflammation: bleeding, meningitis
- Not classified as epilepsy
- Treat the underlying cause.

## Seizures

Unprovoked seizure

- Absence of a provoking clinical condition
- Preexisting brain lesion or progressive nervous system disorder

<!-- image -->

## Seizure: Get a Detailed History!

- Time of day/setting?
- What was the child doing?
- Any new medications?
- Any systemic symptoms?
- Was there an aura?
- What was the first sign of seizure activity?

## Epilepsy

- Enduring predisposition to recurrent seizures
- Two unprovoked seizures >24 hours apart
- One unprovoked with potential for more
- How long did the seizure last?
- Was there a loss of alertness?
- Was there a loss of bowel/bladder?
- Was there a postictal phase? How long did it last?

## QUESTION #11

A 2-year-old child is found to have a microcytic hypochromic anemia. Serum iron and ferritin levels are decreased. Which statement is correct regarding lead toxicity?

1. Lead toxicity is more common in children greater than 6 years of age.
2. This child is more susceptible to toxic effects due to an incomplete blood-brain barrier.
3. Patients with lead toxicity are asymptomatic unless there is moderate to high exposure.
4. Children who live in rural areas have a higher risk of lead poisoning.

## Lead Toxicity

## Masquerades as an iron-deficiency anemia!

- Exposure: dust from old house paint, water, food, lead pipes, sucking on toys, jewelry, and others
- Symptoms
- $ Fatigue, GI (stomachache, constipation), irritability, renal changes
- $ Cognitive and behavioral changes are irreversible.

## Bilirubin

- Predictable pattern in neonates
- $ Full-term: peaks 3-4 days
- $ Premature: peaks 5-7 days (greater risk of bilirubin toxicity)
- Threshold: risk level classified by age vs. serum bilirubin level
- Breastfeeding exaggerates physiologic jaundice.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## Pathological Jaundice: Causes

## Increased production due to hemolysis

- ABO incompatibility, sepsis, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase [G6PD] deficiency, infants with macrosomia

## NOTES

## NOTES Decreased removal of bilirubin due to enzyme deficit or maternal/fetal endocrine problems

- Crigler-Najjar syndrome, Gilbert syndrome

## Increased enterohepatic circulation of bilirubin

- Inadequate feeding, breastfed babies, intestinal obstruction

## Thresholds for Treatment

- Asymptomatic: use risk calculator to determine threshold for intervention
- $ Based on gestational age, postnatal age, stability
- $ Phototherapy is first-line.
- Symptomatic: total bilirubin >25-32 mg/dL
- $ Free bilirubin crosses blood-brain barrier.
- $ Irreversible neurologic dysfunction
- $ BIND = bilirubin-induced neurologic dysfunction
- $ Escalation of care and exchange transfusion

## BIND: Clinical Signs

Clinical signs: BIND (bilirubin-induced neurologic dysfunction) score

## Mental status

- Sleepy but arousable, decreased feeding, poor suck, irritable

## Muscle tone

- Persistent hypotonia; hypertonia

## Cry pattern

- High pitched when aroused; shrill, difficult to console, inconsolable, weak/absent cry

## G6PD Deficiency

- G6PD is an enzyme that protects red blood cells.
- X-linked genetic disorder:
- $ May result in RBC damage or hemolysis
- $ May remain asymptomatic for life
- Newborns with severe jaundice should be screened.
- Screen if positive family history
- Anemia varies depending on deficiency.
- $ Prevalent in tropical and subtropical zones: Africa, Europe, Asia
- Kurdish Jewish (70%), Sardinian (4-35%), Nigerian (22%), Thai (17%), African American (12%), and more

## G6PD Deficiency Presentation

- Asymptomatic
- Acute hemolytic anemia
- $ Triggered by "oxidative stress injury"
- Illness/infection
- Medications: fluoroquinolones, nitrofurantoin, phenazopyridine (Pyridium), sulfonylureas (glipizide, glyburide)
- Chemical exposures/foods: fava beans, henna compounds, naphthalene (mothballs, lavatory deodorant); RUSH "poppers" (energy drinks)
- Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole: probably safe

## Sickle Cell Disease (SCD)

- Normal RBCs are biconcave discs.
- SCD RBCs are sickle-shaped.
- $ Inefficient carriers of O 2 ➔ low O 2 saturation
- $ Tend to clump together ➔ occlusion
- Clinical manifestations
- $ Hemolytic anemia and vaso-occlusion
- Acute/chronic pain
- Tissue ischemia/infarction
- Affects every body system

<!-- image -->

NOTES

## NOTES Sickle Cell Disease (SCD)

- Highly susceptible to infection due to functional asplenia
- Prevention of infection
- $ Precipitate SC crisis
- $ Prophylactic penicillin BID in children
- $ Fever can be life-threatening
- Good nutrition and hydration

## Failure of Bone Marrow = Abnormal RBC, WBC, Platelet Counts

<!-- image -->

## Leukemia

- Cancer of the bone marrow ➔ abnormal RBCs, WBCs, and/or platelets
- Most common form of cancer in children
- Two types of leukemia predominate in children
- $ Acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL): 77%
- $ Acute myelogenous leukemia (AML): 11%
- Most common ages are 2-8 years
- $ Peak occurrence at 4 years
- $ Can occur at any age

## Leukemia: Common Symptoms

- Anorexia, weight loss
- Fever
- Hepatosplenomegaly (>60%)
- Bleeding (50%)
- $ Platelet count less than 100,000
- Persistent bone pain (21-38%)
- $ Long bones: site of bone marrow!
- Lymphadenopathy (50%)

## NOTES

## NOTES Lymph Nodes

## Consider malignancy if:

- Enlarged
- Nontender
- Firm
- Rubbery/matted
- Fixed to underlying tissue

## Leukemia-Diagnostic Tests

- CBC with differential
- $ Thrombocytopenia present 85% of time
- $ WBC may be normal or elevated, lymphoblasts
- $ Anemia
- Peripheral smear: myeloid or lymphoid cells
- Bone marrow aspirate: infiltration with blast cells

## Children's Airways

- Pediatric airways are teeny tiny!
- Constriction or obstruction can cause a big problem!
- Lower respiratory tract infection: bronchitis, bronchiolitis
- CAP: may include the parenchyma, alveolar spaces, and/or interstitial tissue.

## Pneumonia

- Most common pathogens
- $ VIRUSES! <1 year to <5 years
- RSV: new vaccine!
- $ If bacteria-S. pneumoniae (DRSP common)
- $ >5 years: S. pneumoniae ➔ M. pneumoniae

## Pneumococcal Prevention

- Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine
- $ PCV 15 or 20: four doses by age 18 months
- $ Infants are vulnerable and need protection!
- High-risk children >2 years old:
- $ PCV 13 plus PPSV 23

## QUESTION #19

Which of the following is the preferred treatment for the previous 4-year-old patient?

1. Doxycycline 100 mg BID ×10 days
2. Amoxicillin with clavulanate 45 mg/kg/d once daily
3. Azithromycin 10 mg/kg days 1-5

## Pharmacologic Management

- First-line: High-dose amoxicillin (90 mg/kg/d)
- Alternatives
- $ Recent antibiotic exposure: amoxicillin-clavulanate or a third-generation cephalosporin
- $ Penicillin allergy: macrolide (clindamycin)
- Avoid doxycycline <8 years!
- Avoid fluoroquinolones if <18 years!

## Symptomatic Management

- Fluids
- Antipyretics
- Rest
- Hospitalize/oxygen if respiratory distress!

- Recommended annually >6 months
- Initial dosing <8 years

## Bronchiolitis: Presentation

- Fever (lower temps with RSV, higher temps with adenovirus)
- Cough: may be hoarse before becoming very productive
- Thick, purulent nasal secretions
- Respiratory distress if severe bronchiolitis

A 12-month-old child has been diagnosed with bronchiolitis. The child has nasal flaring, retractions, and poor appetite. How should this patient be managed?

3. As an inpatient because of their symptoms
4. As an inpatient because of their age

## Bronchiolitis Management

## Management is usually supportive

- Education and anticipatory guidance
- Suction nose
- Monitor for dehydration
- No bronchodilators (BD)
- No steroids
- $ Modest short-term clinical improvement; does not affect overall outcome

Inpatient management for hydration and respiratory support (e.g., fluids, nasal suctioning, supplemental oxygen).

## Croup

- Also called laryngotracheitis
- Viral croup most common in children aged 6 months to 3 years
- Fever, inspiratory stridor, barking cough, hoarseness (spasmodic at night)
- Self-limited: 3 days
- Steeple sign = tapering of upper trachea on AP radiograph

## Asthma

- Most common chronic illness in children
- Frequent cause of missed school days
- History
- $ Symptom patterns
- $ Precipitating factors
- $ Family history/personal history of atopic diseases

## Suspected Diagnosis <5 years

<!-- image -->

## Asthma: Treatment

- Similar principles of treatment as for adults
- A few key differences
- $ MART therapy with ICS/formoterol not routinely recommended for children younger than 5 years
- $ Mode of drug administration
- $ Leukotriene receptor antagonists (LTRA)
- Neuropsychiatric adverse events
- Risk factors
- $ Sensitivity in certain environments
- $ Sensitivity to animals, smoke, perfumes, etc.
- $ Seasonal
- $ Medications

## NOTES

## NOTES Cystic Fibrosis

- Affects 1 in 2,000 to 3,000 infants
- Routine newborn screening in all 50 states
- $ Sweat chloride test
- Autosomal recessive genetic disorder
- Excessive loss of sodium through sweat
- CFTR channels do not effectively export chloride ➔ thickening of mucus
- Multisystem disease
- $ GI tract
- $ Lungs
- $ Reproductive tract
- $ Sweat glands

<!-- image -->

## QUESTION #27

Which of the following symptoms might be present in a child who has suspected cystic fibrosis?

1. Excessive sweating
2. Frequent episodes of diarrhea
3. Persistent productive cough
4. Persistent watery eyes and tears

## Cystic Fibrosis: Manifestations
